difficulty.rationale: Standard multi-part FRQ on RL growth: qualitative graph with labeled asymptote and time constant, loop-rule derivation with a separable exponential ODE, short numerical evaluation with clean numbers (tau = 25 ms, I about 0.26 A, dI/dt = 12 A/s), and a proportional-reasoning prediction for doubled L. All content is in scope and the wording is unambiguous. Difficulty comes from concept integration across four parts, not from arithmetic or reading.

answers.brief_reasoning: I starts at 0 with its steepest slope, ε/L, then rises in a concave-down curve toward the horizontal asymptote I = ε/R = 0.3 A. At t = τ = L/R = 10 ms the current reaches 0.63ε/R. By 5τ = 50 ms it is about 99% of ε/R.
answers.final_answer: Curve rising from 0 like an exponential approach to the asymptote ε/R = 0.3 A. Mark τ = L/R = 10 ms, where I ≈ 0.63ε/R.

answers.brief_reasoning: Loop rule: ε − IR − L dI/dt = 0. Separate variables: dI/(ε − IR) = dt/L. Integrate from I = 0 at t = 0: −(1/R) ln[(ε − IR)/ε] = t/L. Solve for I.
τ = L/R = 0.4/40 = 0.01 s. At t = 20 ms = 2τ: I = 0.3(1 − e^−2) ≈ 0.259 A. At t = 0, I = 0, so the resistor has no voltage across it and L dI/dt = ε, giving dI/dt = 12/0.4.
answers.final_answer: I(20 ms) ≈ 0.26 A; dI/dt at t = 0 = 30 A/s

answers.brief_reasoning: In steady state dI/dt = 0, so the inductor has no voltage across it and I = ε/R, which does not depend on L. The time to reach 63% of the final current is one time constant, τ = L/R, so doubling L doubles that time.
answers.final_answer: The final current does not change (still 0.3 A). The time to reach 63% doubles (factor of 2), from 10 ms to 20 ms.

difficulty.label: exam_prep
difficulty.rationale: Standard multi-part RL growth item. It combines a qualitative graph sketch with labeled asymptote and time constant, a loop-rule derivation requiring separation of variables and an exponential integral, a short numerical evaluation (t/tau = 2, dI/dt = emf/L), and a proportional-reasoning prediction about doubling L. Concept depth is moderate and typical of an AP free-response question. Arithmetic is light, wording is clear, and the content is in scope.

answers.brief_reasoning: Equipment: two identical flat square metal plates, each 200 cm², held parallel in a vacuum chamber or in air (air is a close approximation). Use a capacitance meter (or an LCR meter), and set the gap with insulating spacers of known thickness or a micrometer screw stage. Procedure: connect the meter leads to the plates and set the separation d with spacers of known thickness. Measure d with calipers or a micrometer and record C. Change the independent variable d through 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 4 mm, keeping the area and alignment the same each time, and record C at every d. To reduce the uncertainty in d: use precision-ground spacers or a micrometer, measure the gap at several points around the edges and average, and repeat each trial. It also helps to subtract the stray capacitance of the leads, found by measuring with the plates far apart.
answers.final_answer: Capacitance meter plus parallel plates with insulating spacers or a micrometer. Vary d with spacers, measure d with calipers or a micrometer, and record C at each d. Reduce the uncertainty in d with precision spacers, by averaging several measurements of the gap, and by repeating trials.

answers.brief_reasoning: C = ε0·A·(1/d). This is linear in 1/d and passes through the origin, with slope ε0·A.
answers.final_answer: Vertical axis: C. Horizontal axis: 1/d. The slope equals ε0·A.

answers.brief_reasoning: Points as (1/d in m⁻¹, C in pF): (1000, 179.01), (667, 119.32), (500, 90.01), (333, 59.13), (250, 44.8). The data are nearly linear and pass through the origin.
answers.final_answer: Horizontal axis: 1/d (m⁻¹), scale 0–1000. Vertical axis: C (pF), scale 0–180. Plot the five points and draw a best-fit line through about the origin with slope ≈ 0.179 pF·m.

answers.brief_reasoning: The least-squares slope (line through the origin) is 1.79×10⁻¹³ F·m. A check using two points on the line, (1000 m⁻¹, 179 pF) and (250 m⁻¹, 44.8 pF), gives slope = (179 − 44.8)×10⁻¹² F ÷ 750 m⁻¹ ≈ 1.79×10⁻¹³ F·m. Then ε0 = slope/A = 1.79×10⁻¹³ F·m ÷ 0.0200 m² ≈ 8.95×10⁻¹² F/m. This is within about 1% of the accepted value. The phrase 'total area' is taken to mean the area of each plate. If it meant the two plates combined, each plate would be 100 cm² and the result would be about twice as large, which does not match the accepted value.
answers.final_answer: ε0 ≈ 8.95×10⁻¹² F/m (C²/N·m²)

answers.brief_reasoning: Equipment: two square metal plates, each 20 cm × 20 cm, held parallel. Use insulating spacers or a micrometer stage to set the gap, and a capacitance meter (LCR meter) to measure C. Set d with spacers of known thickness and check it with calipers or a micrometer at several points. Change d over 1–4 mm and record C at each value. To reduce uncertainty in d: measure the gap at several places, average the readings, and repeat each setting. Also use short, fixed leads and subtract the stray capacitance measured with the plates far apart.
answers.final_answer: Measure C with a capacitance meter while setting d with calibrated insulating spacers or a micrometer. Vary d from 1 to 4 mm. Reduce the uncertainty in d by averaging micrometer readings taken at several points and by repeating trials.

answers.brief_reasoning: Since C = ε0A(1/d), C is linear in 1/d and the slope is ε0A.
answers.final_answer: Vertical axis: C. Horizontal axis: 1/d. The slope equals ε0A.

answers.brief_reasoning: Points to plot, with 1/d in mm⁻¹ and C in pF: (1.00, 349.39), (0.667, 239.12), (0.500, 178.03), (0.333, 117.63), (0.250, 87.14). A least-squares fit gives a slope of about 350 pF·mm and an intercept of about 1.5 pF.
answers.final_answer: Plot C (pF) against 1/d (mm⁻¹), with x from 0 to 1.0 and y from 0 to 360. The best-fit line passes close to the origin and has slope ≈ 350 pF·mm.

answers.brief_reasoning: Slope = 350.4 pF·mm = 3.504×10⁻¹³ F·m. Then ε0 = slope/A = 3.504×10⁻¹³ / 0.0400 m² ≈ 8.76×10⁻¹² F/m. This takes A = 400 cm² as the area of each plate.
answers.flaw_note: "Total area 400 cm²" is unclear: it could mean the combined area of both plates. If so, each plate would be 200 cm² and ε0 would come out about 1.75×10⁻¹¹ F/m, which is unreasonable. So I treated 400 cm² as the area of each plate.
answers.final_answer: ε0 ≈ 8.8×10⁻¹² F/m (about 8.76×10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²))

answers.brief_reasoning: Disagree. As the rod moves, the magnetic flux through the circuit changes, which induces an emf (BLv) and a current I = BLv/R. Because the rod carries current in a magnetic field, it feels a magnetic force of size BIL. By Lenz's law this force points against the motion. For the net force to be zero at constant velocity, an external force equal and opposite to this magnetic force is needed. Energy also requires it: the resistor dissipates power I²R, so work must be done on the rod.
answers.final_answer: Disagree: an induced current produces a retarding magnetic force BIL, so an external force equal to it is needed to keep the net force zero.

answers.brief_reasoning: emf = BLv, so I = BLv/R. The magnetic force on the rod is F = BIL = B²L²v/R. At constant speed the external force must equal this. Substituting: F = (0.5)²(1)²(5)/4 = 0.3125 N.
answers.final_answer: F = B²L²v/R ≈ 0.31 N

answers.brief_reasoning: P = Fv = B²L²v²/R, which is proportional to v². Equivalently, both the emf and the current double, so I²R becomes 4 times larger. At twice the speed, the power is 4 times as large.
answers.final_answer: The power increases by a factor of 4.
